# Korea Public Holidays 2027: Dates, Long Weekends and What Closes

URL: https://realkoreatrip.com/korea-public-holidays-2027/
Last checked: 2026-10-27

## Quick answer

- Korea's two big holidays in 2027 are Seollal (Lunar New Year), February 6–9 with a substitute day, and Chuseok, September 14–16. Many department stores, malls and restaurants close on the main day or for part of these holidays.
- The official calendar lists ten breaks of three days or more in 2027 for a five-day workweek, including long weekends like May 1–3, July 17–19 and October 9–11; Chuseok falls on Tuesday to Thursday.
- For Seollal and Chuseok trains, check Korail's holiday booking notice: holiday tickets go on sale in a separate booking period and sell out quickly. Subways and city buses run as usual.

**In 2027, Seollal (Lunar New Year) falls on February 6–8 with a substitute holiday on February 9, and Chuseok on September 14–16; the official calendar counts ten breaks of three days or more for a five-day workweek.** These are official public holidays for government offices. Many businesses follow them, but shops and restaurants set their own hours, and the biggest closures come at Seollal and Chuseok.

Below: every nationwide 2027 holiday, the 3+ day breaks, and what holidays change for a trip.

Source: [Korea AeroSpace Administration — 2027 calendar](https://www.kasa.go.kr/prog/plcyBrf/brief/kor/sub01_01_04/view.do?plcyBrfNo=431) (Korean, Jun 29, 2026); checked Oct 27, 2026.

![Graphic: Korea 2027 at a glance — Seollal Feb 6–9, Chuseok Sep 14–16, ten 3+ day breaks, check holiday train booking](/img/holidays-steps.png?v=c2b4db1b "Korea's 2027 holidays at a glance. Details and sources below.")

## Nationwide public holidays in 2027

| Date (2027) | Holiday | Substitute day off |
|---|---|---|
| Jan 1 (Fri) | New Year's Day | — |
| Feb 6–8 (Sat–Mon) | **Seollal** (Lunar New Year) | Feb 9 (Tue) |
| Mar 1 (Mon) | Independence Movement Day | — |
| May 1 (Sat) | Labor Day | May 3 (Mon) |
| May 5 (Wed) | Children's Day | — |
| May 13 (Thu) | Buddha's Birthday | — |
| Jun 6 (Sun) | Memorial Day | — |
| Jul 17 (Sat) | Constitution Day | Jul 19 (Mon) |
| Aug 15 (Sun) | Liberation Day | Aug 16 (Mon) |
| Sep 14–16 (Tue–Thu) | **Chuseok** | — |
| Oct 3 (Sun) | National Foundation Day | Oct 4 (Mon) |
| Oct 9 (Sat) | Hangeul Day | Oct 11 (Mon) |
| Dec 25 (Sat) | Christmas Day | Dec 27 (Mon) |

Labor Day and Constitution Day became public holidays in 2026. In all, the official 2027 calendar has 72 public holidays, including Sundays.

Source: [Korea AeroSpace Administration](https://www.kasa.go.kr/prog/plcyBrf/brief/kor/sub01_01_04/view.do?plcyBrfNo=431) and [Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute](https://astro.kasi.re.kr/kor/life/post/calendarData?year=2027) (Korean); checked Oct 27, 2026.

## Ten breaks of three days or more

For institutions on a five-day workweek, the official calendar lists these ten. Most are long weekends; Chuseok falls on Tuesday to Thursday.

| Dates (2027) | Days | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Jan 1–3 | 3 | New Year's Day + weekend |
| Feb 6–9 | 4 | Seollal + substitute day |
| Feb 27 – Mar 1 | 3 | Weekend + Independence Movement Day |
| May 1–3 | 3 | Labor Day + substitute day |
| Jul 17–19 | 3 | Constitution Day + substitute day |
| Aug 14–16 | 3 | Liberation Day + substitute day |
| Sep 14–16 | 3 | Chuseok |
| Oct 2–4 | 3 | National Foundation Day + substitute day |
| Oct 9–11 | 3 | Hangeul Day + substitute day |
| Dec 25–27 | 3 | Christmas + substitute day |

Travel demand surges during major holidays, the Korea Tourism Organization says, so book intercity transport early.

Source: [Korea AeroSpace Administration](https://www.kasa.go.kr/prog/plcyBrf/brief/kor/sub01_01_04/view.do?plcyBrfNo=431) (Korean); checked Oct 27, 2026.

## What holidays change for your trip

| | What to expect |
|---|---|
| Intercity trains and express buses | Sell out quickly at major holidays. For Seollal and Chuseok, don't assume the normal booking window: Korail runs a separate holiday booking period (for Chuseok 2026, on a dedicated page in KORAIL+ and on korail.com, for Korail members only). Check Korail's holiday notice for your dates |
| Subways and city buses | Run as usual through the holiday |
| Shops and restaurants | Hours vary. Many department stores, malls and restaurants close on the main day or for part of Seollal and Chuseok; convenience stores and shops near tourist sites often stay open |
| National museums | Generally closed on Chuseok Day itself (2026 example), open the rest of the holiday |
| Palaces | A palace whose regular closing day falls on a public holiday opens that day and closes on the first non-holiday afterward. In 2026, palaces and museums offered free admission over Chuseok; check the 2027 notices before relying on free admission |

Check opening hours on Naver Map or KakaoMap before you go.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — 2026 Chuseok Holiday Travel Guide](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=1593350), [Visit Seoul — National Holidays](https://english.visitseoul.net/essential-Info-article/National-Holidays_/390) (Seollal and Chuseok closures), [Royal Palaces and Tombs Center](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R702000000.do) (Korean) , [Korail — 2026 Chuseok booking](https://info.korail.com/info/selectBbsNttView.do?bbsNo=199&key=911&nttNo=27180) (Korean) and our [KTX booking guide](/how-to-book-ktx-korea/); checked Oct 28, 2026. Weather by month: [best time to visit Korea](/best-time-to-visit-korea/).

> **Local tip:** At Chuseok, look for songpyeon: half-moon rice cakes filled with soybeans, sesame seeds or red beans and steamed over a bed of pine needles, which gives them a subtle fragrance. The Korea Tourism Organization says you can find them, along with jeon, japchae and yakgwa, at traditional markets, rice cake shops and Korean restaurants. Many places close on the main holiday day, so look in the days around it.

> **Our take:** If you're flexible, avoid arriving on the main days of Seollal or Chuseok and plan city sightseeing then instead of long train trips. If you want to see holiday events, the days around Chuseok are a good time for palaces and museums.

## Before you go

1. Check whether your dates overlap Seollal (Feb 6–9) or Chuseok (Sep 14–16).
2. Traveling by train at Seollal or Chuseok? Check Korail's holiday booking notice for the dates and channel, and book as soon as it opens.
3. Expect some shops and restaurants to close on the main holiday days.
4. Check palace and museum days on their official pages before you go.
5. Need help? The 1330 Korea Travel Helpline runs daily from 07:00 to midnight Korea time.

Source: the official pages above and our [emergency help guide](/emergency-help-korea/); checked Oct 27, 2026.

## FAQ

### When is Seollal (Korean New Year) in 2027?

Seollal falls on Sunday, February 7, 2027. The holiday runs February 6–8, with a substitute holiday on Tuesday, February 9.

### When is Chuseok in 2027?

Chuseok is Wednesday, September 15, 2027, and the holiday runs September 14–16.

### Are shops closed on Korean holidays?

Many department stores, malls and restaurants close on the main day or for part of Seollal and Chuseok. Convenience stores and shops near tourist sites often stay open. On other public holidays, hours vary by business, so check before you go.

### Do subways run on Korean public holidays?

Yes. Subways and city buses run as usual during the holidays.

### How many public holidays does Korea have in 2027?

The official 2027 calendar counts 72 nationwide public holidays including Sundays, and ten breaks of three days or more for a five-day workweek.

# Gyeongbokgung Palace Guide: Hours, Tickets, Free Hanbok Entry and the Guard Ceremony

URL: https://realkoreatrip.com/gyeongbokgung-palace-guide/
Last checked: 2026-10-26

## Quick answer

- Gyeongbokgung normally closes on Tuesdays (if a Tuesday is a public or substitute holiday, it opens that day and closes on the first non-holiday afterward). Hours change by season: in Nov–Feb it's 09:00–17:00, with last entry at 16:00.
- Foreign adults (19–64) pay ₩3,000. Entry is free for foreign visitors aged 18 and under or 65 and over, and for anyone wearing hanbok (top and bottom), Korean or not.
- Arrive by 10:00 for the gate guard ceremony, held at 10:00 and 14:00 (about 20 minutes). Free English tours start at 11:00, 13:30 and 15:30.

**Gyeongbokgung, Seoul's main royal palace, normally closes on Tuesdays (a holiday Tuesday moves the closure to the first non-holiday afterward), and foreign adults (19–64) pay ₩3,000; entry is free if you're 18 or under, 65 or over, or wearing hanbok.** Hours run 09:00–17:00 in Nov–Feb, 09:00–18:00 in Mar–May and Sep–Oct, and 09:00–18:30 in Jun–Aug, with last entry an hour before closing. The gate guard ceremony is at 10:00 and 14:00.

Built in 1395 as the Joseon dynasty's official palace, it is the largest of Seoul's five palaces, according to the Korea Tourism Organization. Below: hours, tickets, the hanbok rule, tours, the ceremony and a short route.

Source: [Royal Palaces and Tombs Center](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R702000000.do?schGroupCode=gbg) (Korean), [Korea Heritage Service Foundation](https://www.kh.or.kr/cms/content/view/221) (Korean) and [Korea Tourism Organization](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=87740); checked Oct 26, 2026.

![Graphic: Gyeongbokgung at a glance — usually closed Tuesdays (holiday exception), ₩3,000 for foreign adults, free in hanbok, guard ceremony 10:00 and 14:00](/img/gyeongbokgung-steps.png?v=148e1cb1 "Gyeongbokgung at a glance. Details and sources below.")

## The short version

| | Gyeongbokgung Palace |
|---|---|
| Closed | Usually Tuesdays; if a Tuesday is a public or substitute holiday, it opens and closes on the first non-holiday afterward |
| Hours | Nov–Feb 09:00–17:00 · Mar–May, Sep–Oct 09:00–18:00 · Jun–Aug 09:00–18:30 |
| Last entry | 1 hour before closing (16:00, 17:00 or 17:30) |
| Ticket | Foreign adults 19–64: ₩3,000 (₩2,400 each in a group of 10 or more) |
| Free | Foreign visitors 18 and under or 65 and over; anyone in hanbok; bring proof of age |
| Guard ceremony | 10:00 and 14:00, about 20 minutes |
| English tour | Free, 11:00, 13:30 and 15:30 (not Tuesdays) |
| Getting there | Gyeongbokgung Station (Line 3), Exit 5: about a 2-minute walk |

Source: [Royal Palaces and Tombs Center — hours](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R702000000.do?schGroupCode=gbg), [fees](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R703000000.do?schGroupCode=gbg), [tours](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R706010000.do?schGroupCode=gbg) and [directions](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R707000000.do?schGroupCode=gbg) (Korean); checked Oct 26, 2026.

> **Local tip:** From Oct 29 to Nov 15, 2026, the palace is free for everyone during the Korea Grand Festival, except on Tuesdays, when it stays closed. Source: [palace notice, Sep 30, 2026](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R403000000.do?schM=view&id=20260930144202825885&schBcid=notice01) (Korean).

## Hours and closing day

| Months | Open | Last entry |
|---|---|---|
| January–February, November–December | 09:00–17:00 | 16:00 |
| March–May, September–October | 09:00–18:00 | 17:00 |
| June–August | 09:00–18:30 | 17:30 |

The regular closing day is Tuesday. If a Tuesday falls on a public holiday or substitute holiday, the palace opens that day and closes on the first non-holiday after it.

Source: [Royal Palaces and Tombs Center — hours](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R702000000.do?schGroupCode=gbg) (Korean); checked Oct 26, 2026.

## Tickets and free entry

| Who | Price |
|---|---|
| Foreign adults, 19–64 | ₩3,000 |
| Groups of 10 or more (19–64) | ₩2,400 per person |
| Foreign visitors 18 and under, or 65 and over | Free (bring ID showing your age) |
| Anyone wearing hanbok | Free |
| Combined palace ticket | ₩6,000: one entry each to the four main palaces and Jongmyo Shrine within 6 months (not the Huwon garden at Changdeokgung) |

Two things to know:

- **The free entry for those aged 24 or under that you may read about is for Korean nationals.** For foreign visitors, the free age is 18 and under.
- **Gyeongbokgung is not part of the free "Culture Day" on Wednesdays.** The palace office lists Gyeongbokgung as an exception.

Source: [Royal Palaces and Tombs Center — admission fees](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R703000000.do?schGroupCode=gbg) (Korean); checked Oct 26, 2026.

## Free entry in hanbok: what counts

The palace office confirms that foreign visitors in hanbok get in free, the same as Koreans. Its guidelines:

| Counts as hanbok | Doesn't count |
|---|---|
| Traditional or modern hanbok with a jeogori (top) and a skirt or trousers | A jeogori over jeans, or hanbok bottoms with a T-shirt |
| A jeogori that wraps closed at the collar, with or without ties | A one-piece hanbok dress without a jeogori |
| A jeogori with a wrap skirt, if the top reaches the waist | A durumagi (long coat) on its own |

The office also asks for hanbok that suits the dignity of the palace, with no excessive exposure.

Source: [Royal Palaces and Tombs Center — free entry in hanbok guidelines](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R705000000.do?schGroupCode=gbg) (Korean); checked Oct 26, 2026.

## What to see

![The two-tiered Geunjeongjeon throne hall behind a stone courtyard at Gyeongbokgung](/img/photo-gyeongbokgung-geunjeongjeon.jpg?v=8ecc8192 "Geunjeongjeon Hall, June 2024. Photo: Basile Morin (CC BY-SA 4.0), cropped.")

| Place | What it is |
|---|---|
| Geunjeongjeon Hall | The throne hall; the Korea Tourism Organization notes its sculptures as examples of Joseon-era technique |
| Gyeonghoeru Pavilion | A royal banquet pavilion on a pond; the present building was rebuilt in 1867 |
| Hyangwonjeong Pavilion | A pavilion and pond inside the palace grounds |
| National Palace Museum of Korea | On the west side of the area outside Heungnyemun Gate |
| National Folk Museum of Korea | East of Hyangwonjeong Pavilion |

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — Gyeongbokgung Palace](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=87740); checked Oct 26, 2026.

![Gyeonghoeru Pavilion on stone pillars, reflected in its pond](/img/photo-gyeongbokgung-gyeonghoeru.jpg?v=0e097b35 "Gyeonghoeru Pavilion, November 2018. Photo: © Frank Schulenburg / CC BY-SA 4.0, cropped.")

The palace burned during the Imjin War (1592–1598), and its buildings were later restored under King Gojong, the Korea Tourism Organization says. Separate interior visits to Gyeonghoeru and Hyangwonjeong are seasonal and need advance online booking. The program is in Korean only and is for ages 7 and over; children aged 6 or under can't enter or accompany a visitor, and the palace says visitors who can't follow the Korean commentary can't enter Gyeonghoeru. Check eligibility and dates on the [palace's tour page](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R706010000.do?schGroupCode=gbg) and [reservation page](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R601000000.do?schGroupCode=gbg) (Korean).

Source: [Korea Heritage Service — Gyeonghoeru](https://www.heritage.go.kr/heri/cul/culSelectDetail.do?ccbaCpno=1111102240000&pageNo=1_1) (Korean; period: 1867, 4th year of King Gojong) and the palace tour page above; checked Oct 26, 2026.

## The gate guard ceremony

![Gate guards in blue robes and black hats holding flags in front of a palace wall](/img/photo-gyeongbokgung-guards.jpg?v=4036a46f "The gate guard ceremony at Gyeongbokgung, November 2019. Photo: Ethan Doyle White (CC BY-SA 4.0), cropped.")

| Event | Time | Length |
|---|---|---|
| Royal Guard Changing Ceremony | 10:00 and 14:00 | About 20 minutes |
| Gwanghwamun gate watch ceremony | 11:00 and 13:00 | About 10 minutes |
| Open guard training | 09:35 and 13:35 | About 15 minutes |

It takes place around Gwanghwamun Gate and the square in front of Heungnyemun Gate. The ceremony has run since 2002, based on records from 1469. The organizers ask you not to touch the guards' flags and weapons or talk to the guards when taking photos, and not to walk between the guards during the ceremony.

Source: [Korea Heritage Service Foundation — program](https://www.kh.or.kr/cms/content/view/221) and [visitor notes](https://www.kh.or.kr/cms/content/view/223) (Korean); checked Oct 26, 2026.

## Free guided tours

| Language | Start times |
|---|---|
| English | 11:00, 13:30, 15:30 |
| Japanese | 10:00, 14:30 |
| Chinese | 10:30, 15:00 |

The palace office lists English tours every day except Tuesday, when the palace is closed. Tours start in front of the information center inside Heungnyemun Gate. The palace lists the usual duration as 1–1.5 hours. Visitors in groups of fewer than 10 can join without booking; groups of 10 or more foreign visitors book by phone from a week to a day ahead. Tours leave on time, and you can't join after the start. From Oct 29 to Nov 15, 2026, regular tours are shortened by 30 minutes, the palace says. Tour times and routes can change.

Source: [Royal Palaces and Tombs Center — guided tours](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R706010000.do?schGroupCode=gbg) (Korean); checked Oct 26, 2026.

## A short route

The palace office suggests 40-, 60- and 90-minute routes. Its 40-minute route:

1. Heungnyemun Gate
2. Yeongjegyo Bridge
3. Geunjeongjeon Hall
4. Sajeongjeon Hall
5. Sujeongjeon Hall
6. Gyeonghoeru Pavilion

The 90-minute route adds Gangnyeongjeon, Gyotaejeon and Jagyeongjeon halls and ends at Hyangwonjeong Pavilion.

Source: [Royal Palaces and Tombs Center — routes](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R701000000.do?schGroupCode=gbg) (Korean); checked Oct 26, 2026. Getting around Seoul: [subway guide](/seoul-subway-guide/).

## Before you go

1. Check the closing day: usually Tuesday, with the public-holiday exception explained above.
2. Check the season's last entry time: 16:00 in Nov–Feb.
3. Bring ID if you're 18 or under or 65 or over, for free entry.
4. In hanbok? Wear a jeogori with a skirt or trousers to get in free.
5. Arrive by 10:00 or 14:00 for the guard ceremony.
6. Need help in English? The 1330 Korea Travel Helpline runs daily from 07:00 to midnight Korea time.

Source: the palace pages above and our [emergency help guide](/emergency-help-korea/); checked Oct 26, 2026.

## FAQ

### What day is Gyeongbokgung closed?

Usually Tuesday. If a Tuesday is a public or substitute holiday, the palace opens that day and closes on the first non-holiday afterward.

### How much is the Gyeongbokgung ticket for foreigners?

₩3,000 for foreign adults aged 19 to 64. It's free for foreign visitors 18 and under or 65 and over, and for anyone wearing hanbok.

### Can foreigners get in free wearing hanbok?

Yes. The palace office says visitors in hanbok enter free whether they are Korean or not, as long as they wear a jeogori top with a skirt or trousers.

### What time is the changing of the guard at Gyeongbokgung?

At 10:00 and 14:00, for about 20 minutes. A shorter gate watch ceremony runs at 11:00 and 13:00.

### Is there an English tour of Gyeongbokgung?

Yes, free tours start at 11:00, 13:30 and 15:30 in front of the information center inside Heungnyemun Gate, every day except Tuesday. Times can change.

# Korean BBQ for First-Timers: How to Grill, Wrap and Order

URL: https://realkoreatrip.com/korean-bbq-guide/
Last checked: 2026-10-26

## Quick answer

- At a Korean BBQ restaurant (gogi-jip), you grill the meat at your table. Some places have staff grill it for you; most tables have a vent that pulls up the smoke.
- Start with samgyeopsal (grilled pork belly), which the Korea Tourism Organization calls the most popular Korean meat dish. Eat it with salt and sesame oil, or wrapped in lettuce.
- To make a wrap (ssam), put meat on lettuce or a perilla leaf, add ssamjang sauce and eat it in one bite. Finish with soybean paste stew or fried rice.

**At a Korean BBQ restaurant, called a gogi-jip ("meat restaurant"), you grill meat at your table, wrap it in lettuce or a perilla leaf with ssamjang sauce, and eat each wrap in one bite.** The Korea Tourism Organization calls samgyeopsal (grilled pork belly) the most popular Korean meat dish. Most tables have a vent for the smoke, and at some places staff grill the meat for you.

Below: what to order, how to make a wrap, how to finish the meal and how to get help.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — About Korean Food](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=229195) (page dated Jul 25, 2025); checked Oct 26, 2026.

![Graphic: Korean BBQ in four steps — grill at the table, wrap in lettuce, one bite, finish with stew or fried rice](/img/korean-bbq-steps.png?v=80a33a69 "Korean BBQ in four steps. Details and sources below.")

## The short version

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1. Grill | You grill the meat at your table; at some places staff do it and tell you when it's ready |
| 2. Wrap | Meat on lettuce or a perilla leaf, plus ssamjang sauce |
| 3. Eat | The whole wrap in one bite |
| 4. Finish | Doenjang-jjigae (soybean paste stew) or fried rice |
| Need help? | Call out "Yeogiyo!" (Excuse me!) |

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — About Korean Food](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=229195); checked Oct 26, 2026.

![A tabletop grill with raw pork belly, kimchi, bean sprouts and side dishes](/img/photo-korean-bbq-table.jpg?v=e818eeaf "A tabletop grill with raw pork belly, vegetables and side dishes, December 2017. Photo: 이동원 (CC0), cropped.")

## What to order

| Dish | What it is | How it's eaten |
|---|---|---|
| **Samgyeopsal** (grilled pork belly) | Fatty, tender pork belly, one of Koreans' favorite pork cuts | With chili-soybean paste, or sesame oil and salt; in lettuce, or with garlic |
| **Dwaeji-galbi** (pork ribs) | Pork galbi marinated in soy sauce or red chili paste; more affordable than beef ribs | Grilled at the table |
| **Galbi** (beef ribs) | Usually marinated in soy sauce; salt-seasoned galbi is lighter | Grilled |
| **Bulgogi** | Thin beef slices in a marinade made with vegetables and fruit such as onion and pear | Pan-fried; nowadays cooks add broth or water instead of grilling it crisp |

The Korea Tourism Organization adds that some restaurants have a charcoal grill built into the table.

Source: Korea Tourism Organization food guides for [samgyeopsal](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=178546), [pork galbi](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=178496), [salted galbi](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=180109) and [bulgogi](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=178541); checked Oct 26, 2026.

## How to make a wrap (ssam)

1. Take a lettuce or perilla leaf.
2. Add a piece of grilled meat.
3. Add ssamjang, a sauce of red chili paste and soybean paste mixed with garlic, scallions and sesame oil.
4. Open wide and eat it all in one bite: that's the Korea Tourism Organization's tip.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — About Korean Food](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=229195); checked Oct 26, 2026.

> **Our take:** If one bite feels like a lot, use a smaller leaf or less meat. The Korea Tourism Organization's point is to eat each wrap whole rather than biting it in half.

## Finishing the meal

| Dish | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Doenjang-jjigae** | Soybean paste stew with tofu, mushrooms, zucchini and clams, eaten with rice |
| **Fried rice** | Rice fried to finish the meal |

At a gogi-jip you also eat the meat with side dishes, stews and noodles, the Korea Tourism Organization says.

> **Local tip:** The doenjang-jjigae that ends the meal can change with the season. The Korea Tourism Organization's food guide says you can add shepherd's purse or wild chives in spring, or parboiled dried radish leaves in winter.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — About Korean Food](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=229195) and [Soybean Paste Jjigae](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=178309); checked Oct 26, 2026.

## Practical tips

| | What to know |
|---|---|
| Calling staff | Say "Yeogiyo!" (Excuse me!) to order more or ask a question; if there's a call bell, press it |
| Tipping | Not needed; extra water or complimentary side dishes don't cost more (anything you order separately does) |
| Ordering | Menus vary: ask staff how portions are sold, and whether they'll grill or you should |
| Smoke and smells | Most tables have a vent; some chairs open up to store your coat away from food smells |
| Chopsticks | Using a spoon alongside them is fine |
| Outdoor tables | "Yajang," tables set up outside the restaurant, are getting popular |

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — About Korean Food](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=229195); checked Oct 26, 2026. More: [Korean etiquette](/korean-etiquette/) and [Korean street food](/korean-street-food/).

## FAQ

### How do you eat Korean BBQ?

Grill the meat at your table (or let staff do it), put it on a lettuce or perilla leaf with ssamjang sauce, and eat the wrap in one bite. Finish with soybean paste stew or fried rice.

### What is samgyeopsal?

Grilled pork belly. The Korea Tourism Organization calls it the most popular Korean meat dish and suggests eating it with chili-soybean paste, or sesame oil and salt, or wrapped in lettuce.

### What's the difference between galbi and bulgogi?

Galbi is ribs, usually marinated in soy sauce and grilled; pork galbi is a more affordable choice than beef. Bulgogi is thinly sliced, marinated beef that is pan-fried, nowadays with broth or water added.

### Do I have to grill the meat myself?

Not always. At some Korean BBQ restaurants, staff grill the meat for you and tell you when it's ready to eat.

### Do you tip at Korean BBQ restaurants?

No. The Korea Tourism Organization says there's no need to tip at Korean restaurants.

## Sources

- Korea Tourism Organization — About Korean Food: https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=229195
- Korea Tourism Organization — Grilled Pork Belly (Samgyeopsal): https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=178546
- Korea Tourism Organization — Grilled Spareribs (Dwaejigalbi): https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=178496
- Korea Tourism Organization — Bulgogi: https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=178541
- Korea Tourism Organization — Grilled Salted Galbi: https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=180109
- Korea Tourism Organization — Soybean Paste Jjigae (Doenjangjjigae): https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=178309

# Korean Street Food Guide: Tteokbokki, Gimbap, Fish Cakes and Winter Snacks

URL: https://realkoreatrip.com/korean-street-food/
Last checked: 2026-10-26

## Quick answer

- Start with the classic trio: tteokbokki (rice cakes in gochujang sauce), sundae (Korean blood sausage) and fried foods. Koreans call the combination \"tteoktwisun.\"
- Easy first picks: gimbap and fish cakes. Fish cake skewers simmer in anchovy broth and are sold one at a time, the Korea Tourism Organization says. Spicy versions exist, so ask about the fillings or sauce.
- In winter, look for hotteok and bungeoppang (fish-shaped buns with red bean filling). For a market full of food stalls, Gwangjang Market's food street is open until 23:00 and on Sundays.

**Most of the street food visitors run into in Korea is bunsik, the Korea Tourism Organization says: tteokbokki, sundae, gimbap, fish cakes and fried foods, sold at street stalls, snack shops and convenience stores.** Bunsik literally means "food made of flour," but Koreans use it for any quick, simple meal. The Korea Tourism Organization describes bunsik as affordable and suggests ordering several dishes at once.

Below: what each dish is, seasonal snacks, where to find them and how ordering works.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — Bunsik & Street Food](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140730) (page updated Mar 24, 2023); checked Oct 26, 2026.

![Graphic: Korean street food at a glance — tteokbokki, sundae, gimbap, fish cakes, hotteok and bungeoppang in winter](/img/street-food-steps.png?v=0bca2894 "Korean street food at a glance. Details and sources below.")

## The short version

| Dish | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Tteokbokki** | Rice cakes boiled down in gochujang (red chili paste) sauce; cream and ramen versions too |
| **Sundae** | Pig intestines stuffed with glass noodles, sticky rice, vegetables and blood |
| **Gimbap** | Rice and fillings rolled in dried laver (seaweed) and sliced |
| **Fish cakes (eomuk)** | Skewered fish cakes simmered in anchovy broth, sold one at a time |
| **Skewers** | Chicken skewers with sauce, or fried rice cake skewers with sweet-spicy sauce |
| **Hotteok** (winter) | Fried dough filled with sugar and nuts; some have vegetables or cheese |
| **Bungeoppang** (winter) | Fish-shaped bun with red bean or custard filling |

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — Bunsik & Street Food](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140730); checked Oct 26, 2026.

## The classics

![Fish cake skewers simmering in trays next to a pan of tteokbokki at a market stall](/img/photo-street-food-tteokbokki-eomuk.jpg?v=ee58c786 "Fish cakes and tteokbokki at a stall in Pupyeong Market, Busan, February 2009. Photo: Junho Jung (CC BY-SA 3.0), cropped.")

### Tteokbokki

The Korea Tourism Organization calls tteokbokki the center of all bunsik. The usual way to make it is to mix rice cakes with gochujang seasoning and boil them down. You'll also see variations such as cream tteokbokki and ramen tteokbokki.

### Sundae

Pig intestines are stuffed with a mix of minced blood, glass noodles, sticky rice and vegetables. The Korea Tourism Organization compares it to black pudding and haggis. Tteokbokki, sundae and fried foods ordered together are called "tteoktwisun."

### Gimbap

Rice and fillings are laid on a sheet of dried laver, rolled and cut into bite-sized pieces. There are many kinds at many prices, and you can buy it at snack shops, convenience stores, service areas, supermarkets and department store food halls.

### Fish cakes and skewers

![Fish cake skewers folded on wooden sticks in a tray of broth](/img/photo-street-food-eomuk.jpg?v=9db7f0e4 "Fish cake skewers in broth, October 2015. Photo: Choe Kwangmo (CC0), cropped.")

At bunsik stalls, fish cakes are usually skewered, simmered in anchovy broth and sold individually. Skewers also come as chicken with a layer of sauce, or as fried rice cakes brushed with a sweet and spicy sauce.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — Bunsik & Street Food](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140730); checked Oct 26, 2026.

## Seasonal snacks

| Season | Snack | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Winter | Hotteok | Chewy dough filled with raw sugar and nuts, fried in oil |
| Winter | Bungeoppang | Crispy fish-shaped bun with red bean, or custard cream |
| Summer | Kongguksu | Noodles in cold, finely ground soybean soup |
| Summer | Bingsu | Shaved ice with sweet red bean, rice cake and fruit; often summer-only at snack shops |

The Korea Tourism Organization notes that bungeoppang is crispiest right after you buy it from a street cart, and suggests kongguksu as a dish for vegetarians; ask about the broth and toppings to be sure.

> **Local tip:** Look beyond hotteok and bungeoppang, too. The Korea Tourism Organization also lists steamed buns and baked sweet potatoes among the street snacks you can try in specific seasons.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — Bunsik & Street Food](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140730); checked Oct 26, 2026.

## Where to find it

| Where | What to expect |
|---|---|
| Bunsik shops | Snack restaurants serving tteokbokki, gimbap and fried foods |
| Street stalls and carts | Skewers and, in winter, hotteok and bungeoppang |
| Convenience stores | Gimbap and popular snacks |
| Gwangjang Market, Seoul | A food street inside the market, by the East Gate, North Gate 2 and South Gate 1 |

### Gwangjang Market

| | Gwangjang Market |
|---|---|
| Food street | Listed hours: 09:00–23:00, open daily; individual stalls may vary |
| General shops | Listed hours: 09:00–18:00, closed Sundays |
| Vintage / second-hand clothing shops | Listed hours: 10:00–19:00, closed Sundays |
| Address | 88 Changgyeonggung-ro, Jongno-gu, Seoul |

The Korea Tourism Organization calls it Korea's first permanent market. The market's own notice gives the same hours; individual stalls may keep their own.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — Gwangjang Market](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/whereToGo/locIntrdn/rgnContentsView.do?vcontsId=106345) and [Gwangjang Market — opening hours notice](http://www.kwangjangmarket.co.kr/?p=1574) (Korean, 2017); checked Oct 26, 2026. Getting there: [Seoul subway guide](/seoul-subway-guide/).

## Ordering and paying

1. Point at what you want; at fish cake stalls, you usually pay by the skewer.
2. Restaurants don't expect tips, and extra water or complimentary side dishes are free, the Korea Tourism Organization says; anything you order separately is charged.
3. More places now have self-service water and side dishes, or ordering kiosks.
4. If chopsticks are hard to use, a spoon is fine.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — About Korean Food](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=229195) and [Bunsik & Street Food](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140730); checked Oct 26, 2026. More: [Korean etiquette](/korean-etiquette/) and [paying in Korea](/paying-in-korea-foreign-cards-cash/).

> **Our take:** Order two or three different things at once, as the Korea Tourism Organization suggests. Tteokbokki is the one made with chili paste, so try a little first if you're not used to spicy food.

## FAQ

### What is bunsik in Korea?

Bunsik literally means "food made of flour," but it covers any quick, simple meal, such as tteokbokki, sundae, gimbap, fish cakes and fried foods.

### Is tteokbokki spicy?

The usual version is made with gochujang (red chili paste). The Korea Tourism Organization also mentions variations such as cream tteokbokki and ramen tteokbokki.

### When can I find hotteok and bungeoppang?

Mostly in winter. The Korea Tourism Organization describes both as winter street snacks.

### What time is Gwangjang Market's food street open?

The Korea Tourism Organization lists the food street's hours as 09:00–23:00 daily. General shops are listed as 09:00–18:00, while vintage clothing shops are listed as 10:00–19:00; these shops close on Sundays. Individual opening hours may vary.

## Sources

- Korea Tourism Organization — Bunsik & Street Food: https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140730
- Korea Tourism Organization — About Korean Food: https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=229195
- Korea Tourism Organization — Gwangjang Market: https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/whereToGo/locIntrdn/rgnContentsView.do?vcontsId=106345
- Gwangjang Market — Opening hours notice (Korean): http://www.kwangjangmarket.co.kr/

# Best Time to Visit Korea: Month-by-Month Weather

URL: https://realkoreatrip.com/best-time-to-visit-korea/
Last checked: 2026-10-25

## Quick answer

- For mild weather, go in spring or autumn. Seoul averages 12.6°C in April, 18.2°C in May, 21.6°C in September and 15.0°C in October (1991–2020 averages).
- July and August are hot and wet: Seoul averages 25–26°C, and July is its wettest month with 414.4 mm of rain. June to August brings about 63% of the year's rain.
- January is the coldest month, averaging −1.9°C in Seoul (lows around −5.5°C). Busan and Jeju are milder: 3.6°C and 6.1°C on average in January.

**For mild weather in Korea, go in spring (April–May) or autumn (September–October): Seoul averages 12.6–18.2°C in April and May, and 21.6°C and 15.0°C in September and October.** July is the wettest month, with 414.4 mm of rain on average in Seoul, and January the coldest, at −1.9°C. These are the Korea Meteorological Administration's official averages for 1991–2020, not a forecast for any one year.

Source: [Korea Meteorological Administration — climate normals 1991–2020](https://data.kma.go.kr/normals/table.do) and [Seoul regional climate](https://www.weather.go.kr/w/climate/statistics/region.do) (Korean); checked Oct 25, 2026.

![Graphic: Korea's seasons at a glance — spring and autumn mild, summer hot and wet, winter cold and dry, with Seoul averages](/img/season-steps.png?v=eef33158 "Korea's seasons at a glance. Details and sources below.")

## The short version

| Season (Seoul) | Average temperature | Rain | What it means for your trip |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Spring** (March–May) | 6.1°C → 18.2°C | 36.9–103.6 mm a month | Cool to mild; March can still be cold |
| **Summer** (June–August) | 22.7–26.1°C | 892.1 mm in total, about 63% of the year's rain | Hot, humid and wet, especially July |
| **Autumn** (September–November) | 21.6°C → 7.5°C | 141.5 mm in September, then about 50 mm a month | Mild and drier; November turns cold |
| **Winter** (December–February) | −1.9°C to 0.7°C | 67.6 mm in total, about 5% of the year's rain | Cold and dry |

Source: [Korea Meteorological Administration](https://data.kma.go.kr/normals/table.do), 1991–2020 averages for Seoul, and [Seoul regional climate](https://www.weather.go.kr/w/climate/statistics/region.do) (Korean); checked Oct 25, 2026.

## Seoul, month by month

| Month | Average | High | Low | Rain | Humidity |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| January | −1.9°C | 2.1°C | −5.5°C | 16.8 mm | 56% |
| February | 0.7°C | 5.1°C | −3.2°C | 28.2 mm | 55% |
| March | 6.1°C | 11.0°C | 1.9°C | 36.9 mm | 55% |
| April | 12.6°C | 17.9°C | 8.0°C | 72.9 mm | 55% |
| May | 18.2°C | 23.6°C | 13.5°C | 103.6 mm | 60% |
| June | 22.7°C | 27.6°C | 18.7°C | 129.5 mm | 66% |
| July | 25.3°C | 29.0°C | 22.3°C | 414.4 mm | 76% |
| August | 26.1°C | 30.0°C | 22.9°C | 348.2 mm | 74% |
| September | 21.6°C | 26.2°C | 17.7°C | 141.5 mm | 66% |
| October | 15.0°C | 20.2°C | 10.6°C | 52.2 mm | 62% |
| November | 7.5°C | 11.9°C | 3.5°C | 51.1 mm | 60% |
| December | 0.2°C | 4.2°C | −3.4°C | 22.6 mm | 58% |

"High" and "low" are the average daily maximum and minimum. Humidity is rounded to the nearest percent.

Source: [Korea Meteorological Administration — monthly climate normals, Seoul (station 108)](https://data.kma.go.kr/normals/table.do), 1991–2020 (Korean); checked Oct 25, 2026.

## Spring: April and May

![Cherry trees in full white bloom over a path in Seoul Forest, with a tower behind](/img/photo-seoul-cherry-blossoms.jpg?v=8ff4bee7 "Cherry blossoms in Seoul Forest, April 6, 2024. Photo: WANGYIFAN2024 (CC0), cropped.")

- **April:** average 12.6°C (8.0–17.9°C), 72.9 mm of rain.
- **May:** average 18.2°C (13.5–23.6°C), 103.6 mm of rain, and Seoul's sunniest month on average (223 hours of sunshine).
- **March** is still cool: 6.1°C on average, with lows around 1.9°C.

> **Local tip:** Seoul's "official" cherry blossom is a designated standard tree at the Seoul weather station, and the Korea Meteorological Administration's Seoul cherry blossom records go back to 1922. It opens on April 8 on average, but in 2026 it opened on March 29, ten days early. Bloom dates vary from year to year, so check KMA's spring-flower status on its Weather Nuri site (Korean) before you fix your dates.

> **Our take:** April and May are the easiest months for walking-heavy sightseeing. Bring a light jacket for April evenings.

Source: [Korea Meteorological Administration](https://data.kma.go.kr/normals/table.do), Seoul 1991–2020 (Korean); checked Oct 25, 2026. Cherry blossom: [KMA Seoul office press release, March 29, 2026](https://www.weather.go.kr/kma/flexer/html/press/2026/03/29/ATC202603291603412_b86c30ac-d966-46d4-94a2-02c312fb8a7f.hwp.files/Sections1.html) (Korean); checked Oct 30, 2026.

## Summer: June to August

- **Hot and humid:** July averages 25.3°C and August 26.1°C in Seoul, with highs around 29–30°C and humidity around 74–76%.
- **Wet:** July (414.4 mm) and August (348.2 mm) are Seoul's wettest months. June to August together bring 892.1 mm, about 63% of the year's rain.

> **Our take:** If you travel in summer, plan indoor options for rainy days and carry an umbrella. It's the season for Busan's beaches, not long city walks at midday.

Source: [Korea Meteorological Administration](https://data.kma.go.kr/normals/table.do) and [Seoul regional climate](https://www.weather.go.kr/w/climate/statistics/region.do) (Korean); checked Oct 25, 2026. Beaches: [Busan travel guide](/busan-travel-guide/).

## Autumn: September to November

- **September:** average 21.6°C, but still fairly wet (141.5 mm).
- **October:** average 15.0°C (10.6–20.2°C), 52.2 mm of rain, and about as sunny as April (206.5 hours).
- **November:** average 7.5°C. On average, Seoul's first frost comes on October 28 and its first snow on November 20.

> **Our take:** Late September to October is the other sweet spot, with dry, mild days for palaces, hiking and day trips.

Source: [Korea Meteorological Administration](https://data.kma.go.kr/normals/table.do) and [Seoul regional climate](https://www.weather.go.kr/w/climate/statistics/region.do) (Korean); checked Oct 25, 2026.

## Winter: December to February

![Snow-covered Baengnokdam crater at the summit of Hallasan under a blue sky](/img/photo-jeju-hallasan.jpg?v=329a2768 "Baengnokdam, the crater at the top of Hallasan on Jeju, January 2025. Photo: Sadopaul (CC BY 4.0), cropped.")

- **Cold:** January averages −1.9°C in Seoul, with lows around −5.5°C. December averages 0.2°C and February 0.7°C.
- **Dry:** December to February brings only 67.6 mm in total, about 5% of the year's rain.

> **Our take:** Winter is cold and dry. Pack a warm coat, gloves and a hat for Seoul.

Source: [Korea Meteorological Administration](https://data.kma.go.kr/normals/table.do) and [Seoul regional climate](https://www.weather.go.kr/w/climate/statistics/region.do) (Korean); checked Oct 25, 2026.

## Busan and Jeju: warmer in winter

| | Seoul | Busan | Jeju City |
|---|---|---|---|
| January average | −1.9°C | 3.6°C | 6.1°C |
| April average | 12.6°C | 13.8°C | 14.2°C |
| August average | 26.1°C | 26.1°C | 27.2°C |
| October average | 15.0°C | 17.9°C | 18.6°C |
| Wettest month | July, 414.4 mm | July, 326.8 mm | August, 272.3 mm |

Source: [Korea Meteorological Administration — climate normals](https://data.kma.go.kr/normals/table.do), 1991–2020, stations Seoul (108), Busan (159) and Jeju (184) (Korean); checked Oct 25, 2026. Trip ideas: [Busan](/busan-travel-guide/) and [Jeju](/jeju-travel-guide/).

## Holidays: plan around Seollal and Chuseok

Korea's **Seollal** (Lunar New Year) and **Chuseok** holidays are set by the lunar calendar, so their dates on the regular calendar change each year. Holiday KTX trains have their own booking schedule and rules, separate from the normal two-month window, so check Korail's notices and book early if your trip overlaps.

Source: [Korail — 2026 Chuseok reservations notice](https://www.korail.com/global/eng/siteInfo/notice/25622), checked Oct 23, 2026; [Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute — official calendar (almanac)](https://astro.kasi.re.kr/kor/life/post/almanac) (Korean), checked Oct 25, 2026. Details: [how to book the KTX](/how-to-book-ktx-korea/).

## Before you book

1. Pick your season with the month-by-month table above.
2. Traveling June to August? Pack for heat, humidity and heavy rain.
3. Traveling December to February? Pack warm layers; Busan and Jeju are milder than Seoul.
4. Check whether your dates overlap Seollal or Chuseok, and book trains early if they do.
5. Check the forecast a week before you go: averages aren't a forecast.

Source: [Korea Meteorological Administration](https://data.kma.go.kr/normals/table.do); checked Oct 25, 2026.

## FAQ

### What is the best month to visit Korea?

For mild weather, April, May, September and October. Seoul averages 12.6°C, 18.2°C, 21.6°C and 15.0°C in those months (1991–2020 averages).

### What is the rainy season in Korea?

Summer. In Seoul, June to August brings about 63% of the year's rain, and July is the wettest month, with 414.4 mm on average.

### How cold is Korea in winter?

January averages −1.9°C in Seoul, with lows around −5.5°C. Busan (3.6°C) and Jeju (6.1°C) are milder.

### Does it snow in Seoul?

Yes. On average, Seoul's first snow of the season comes on November 20.

## Sources

- Korea Meteorological Administration, Seoul office — Cherry blossom press release, Mar 29, 2026 (Korean): https://www.weather.go.kr/kma/flexer/html/press/2026/03/29/ATC202603291603412_b86c30ac-d966-46d4-94a2-02c312fb8a7f.hwp.files/Sections1.html
- Korea Meteorological Administration — Climate normals 1991–2020 (Korean): https://data.kma.go.kr/normals/table.do
- Korea Meteorological Administration — Regional climate, Seoul and Gyeonggi (Korean): https://www.weather.go.kr/w/climate/statistics/region.do

# Emergency Help in Korea: 112, 119, 1330 and English-Speaking Hospitals

URL: https://realkoreatrip.com/emergency-help-korea/
Last checked: 2026-10-25

## Quick answer

- Emergency? Call 112 for the police or 119 for fire and ambulance. If you don't speak Korean, say \"English please\" or \"Interpreter please\" and the operator connects an interpreter.
- Travel help? Call 1330, the Korea Travel Helpline, daily from 07:00 to midnight Korea time (+82-2-1330 from overseas), for travel information, interpretation and complaints.
- Lost something? Check LOST 112, the police lost-and-found site, at lost112.go.kr (182 from a phone in Korea).

**In an emergency in Korea, call 112 for the police or 119 for fire and ambulance; if you don't speak Korean, say "English please" or "Interpreter please" and the operator connects a professional interpreter.** For travel information and interpretation, call the 1330 Korea Travel Helpline, every day from 07:00 to midnight Korea time (1330 in Korea, +82-2-1330 from overseas). Save these numbers before you fly.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — disaster safety services](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?menuSn=177&vcontsId=248145) and [Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency — 1330 hours](https://kdca.go.kr/KDCAtemp/5289/subview.do) (Korean); checked Oct 25, 2026.

![Graphic: who to call in Korea — 112 police, 119 fire and ambulance, 1330 travel hotline, 182 lost and found](/img/emergency-steps.png?v=b229b19d "Who to call in Korea. Details and sources below.")

## The short version

| Dial in Korea | For | From overseas |
|---|---|---|
| **112** | Police emergencies | — (call 112 while in Korea) |
| **119** | Fire, ambulance and medical emergencies | — (call 119 while in Korea) |
| **1339** | Infectious disease information and reporting (KDCA) | +82-2-2633-1339 or +82-2-2163-5945 |
| **1330** | Korea Travel Helpline, daily 07:00–24:00 Korea time | +82-2-1330 |
| **182** | Police call center (lost property: lost112.go.kr) | — |
| **1345** | Immigration Center: visas and immigration | +82-2-1345 |

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — emergency situations](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140042) (updated Sep 11, 2026), [KDCA call center](https://www.kdca.go.kr/eng/4276/subview.do), [KDCA — 1330 hours](https://kdca.go.kr/KDCAtemp/5289/subview.do) (Korean) and [Seoul Metropolitan Government](https://english.seoul.go.kr/policy/transportation/modes-of-transport/taxi/); checked Oct 25, 2026.

## Calling 112 or 119

Call **112** or **119** when there's a threat to life or property. When the call connects:

1. **Say "English please" or "Interpreter please."** The operator connects you to a professional interpreter.
2. **Say where you are.** Use the names of nearby buildings, or the GPS on your phone.
3. **Describe what happened** and follow the operator's instructions.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — disaster safety services](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?menuSn=177&vcontsId=248145); checked Oct 25, 2026.

> **Local tip:** Take a screenshot of your hotel's address in Korean and your location on a map app. It's much faster than spelling out a street name on the phone.

## Two safety apps worth installing

| App | What it does | Languages |
|---|---|---|
| **Baro Emergency Reporting App** (Ministry of the Interior and Safety) | Report an emergency by text or image, not only by voice | English, Chinese, Japanese, Vietnamese, Filipino and more |
| **Emergency Ready** (Ministry of the Interior and Safety) | Disaster and safety information, with disaster-alert settings for your region | 22 languages, including English, Chinese and Japanese |

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — disaster safety services](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?menuSn=177&vcontsId=248145) (updated Oct 2026) and [Seoul Metropolitan Government — Emergency Ready App](https://english.seoul.go.kr/service/living/disaster-evacuation-tips-citizens/emergency-ready-app/); checked Oct 25, 2026. Download both from Google Play or the App Store.

## 1330: the travel helpline

The **1330 Korea Travel Hotline** is a phone and real-time chat service run by the Korea Tourism Organization. It answers every day from 07:00 to midnight Korea time, in English and several other languages.

| | |
|---|---|
| Helps with | Tourist information, interpretation, complaints and the tourist police |
| Call | 1330 in Korea · +82-2-1330 from overseas |
| Free voice call | Online voice call over Wi-Fi (Android, iOS), linked from the official 1330 page |
| Chat | 1330 Messenger (no download), KakaoTalk, Facebook, Line or WhatsApp |
| Formal complaint | touristcomplaint.or.kr or tourcom@knto.or.kr |

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — 1330 Travel Helpline & Complaint Center](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140632) and [KDCA — 1330 hours](https://kdca.go.kr/KDCAtemp/5289/subview.do) (Korean); checked Oct 25, 2026.

## Seeing a doctor

For a medical emergency, call **119**. For non-urgent care, the Korea Tourism Organization says many of Korea's large hospitals run an **International Health Care Center** with interpreters who help from booking to follow-up. The Korea Tourism Organization lists the centers below with weekday hours; these are the international centers' hours, not the hospitals' emergency departments. Contact the center before visiting.

| Hospital (city) | International center phone | Hours |
|---|---|---|
| Seoul Asan Medical Center (Seoul) | +82-2-3010-5001 (English) | Mon–Fri 08:30–17:30 |
| Severance Hospital (Seoul) | +82-2-2228-5800 | Mon–Fri 08:30–17:30 |
| Samsung Medical Center (Seoul) | +82-2-3410-0200 | Mon–Fri 08:00–17:00 |
| Seoul National University Hospital (Seoul) | +82-2-2072-0505 | Mon–Fri 09:00–17:30 |
| Seoul St. Mary's Hospital (Seoul) | +82-2-2258-5745 | Mon–Fri 08:30–17:00 |
| Kyungpook National University Hospital (Daegu) | +82-53-200-6114 (English) | Mon–Fri 08:30–17:30 |
| Inje University Haeundae Paik Hospital (Busan) | +82-51-797-0566 | Mon–Fri reception 08:00–17:00; clinic 09:00–12:00 and 13:30–17:00 |

This is part of the Korea Tourism Organization's list; it includes more hospitals in Seoul, Incheon, Suwon and Iksan. We list them as published, not as recommendations.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — emergency situations](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140042) (updated Sep 11, 2026) and [Haeundae Paik Hospital — International Healthcare Center](https://www.paik.ac.kr/haeundae_eng/user/contents/view.do?menuNo=600021); checked Oct 25, 2026.

## Lost something?

- **LOST 112**, the National Police Agency's lost-and-found site: lost112.go.kr, in Korean, English, Japanese and Chinese. From a phone in Korea, the police call center is 182.
- Need help explaining what you lost? Call **1330** for interpretation (07:00–midnight).

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — emergency situations](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140042) and [1330 Travel Helpline](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140632); checked Oct 25, 2026.

## Your embassy

If you lose your passport or need consular help, contact your country's embassy. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs lists the diplomatic missions in Korea at mofa.go.kr (Korean and English).

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — emergency situations](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140042); checked Oct 25, 2026.

## Before you fly

1. Save 112, 119 and 1330 (+82-2-1330) in your phone.
2. Install the Baro Emergency Reporting App and the Emergency Ready app.
3. Write down your embassy's phone number and your hotel's address in Korean.
4. If you take regular medicine, note the hospital's international center for the city you'll be in.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?menuSn=177&vcontsId=248145); checked Oct 25, 2026. More preparation: [Korea first-timer checklist](/korea-first-time-checklist/).

## FAQ

### What is the emergency number in Korea?

112 for the police and 119 for fire, ambulance and medical emergencies. If you don't speak Korean, say "English please" or "Interpreter please" and an interpreter joins the call.

### Is there an English helpline for tourists in Korea?

Yes. The 1330 Korea Travel Helpline answers every day from 07:00 to midnight Korea time, in English and other languages: 1330 in Korea, or +82-2-1330 from overseas.

### Where can I see an English-speaking doctor in Korea?

Many large hospitals have an International Health Care Center with interpreters; the ones listed above are open on weekdays. For an emergency, call 119.

### How do I find something I lost in Korea?

Check LOST 112, the police lost-and-found site, at lost112.go.kr. From a phone in Korea you can also call the police call center at 182.

## Sources

- Korea Tourism Organization — Disaster safety services for international visitors: https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?menuSn=177&vcontsId=248145
- Korea Tourism Organization — Emergency situations: https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140042

- Seoul Metropolitan Government — contact numbers: https://english.seoul.go.kr/policy/transportation/modes-of-transport/taxi/

# 10 Apps for Traveling in Korea: What Each One Does

URL: https://realkoreatrip.com/korea-travel-apps/
Last checked: 2026-10-25

## Quick answer

- Install Naver Map and Papago before you fly. Naver Map gives transit, walking and driving directions with English maps; Papago, also by NAVER Corp., translates text, photos and speech across 14 languages (offline only for some languages, after you download a pack).
- For transport: KORAIL+ sells KTX tickets. For taxis, k.ride and TABA take overseas cards registered in the app, and Uber works with your existing account.
- For entry and safety: apply for a K-ETA only on k-eta.go.kr or the official K-ETA app, and add the government's Emergency Ready and Baro Emergency Reporting apps.

**The two apps to install before you fly are Naver Map, for transit, walking and driving directions with English maps, and Papago, NAVER's translator for 14 languages that also reads text from photos.** Add KORAIL+ for KTX tickets, a taxi app that takes overseas cards (k.ride, Uber or TABA), the official K-ETA app if you need one, and the government's two safety apps. Below: what each app does, according to its official listing or operator.

Source: [Naver Map](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/naver-map-navigation/id311867728) and [Papago](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/naver-papago-ai-translator/id1147874819) App Store listings and [Korail](https://www.korail.com/global/eng/passengerGuide/ticketTypes/tickets); checked Oct 25, 2026.

![Graphic: 10 apps for Korea at a glance — maps, translation, trains, entry, taxis, payment, safety](/img/apps-steps.png?v=c177a6e9 "10 apps for Korea at a glance. Details and sources below.")

## The short version

| Need | App | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Maps and directions | **Naver Map** | Transit with real-time departure and arrival times, walking and driving directions; maps in English |
| Translation | **Papago** | Text, photo, voice and conversation translation across 14 languages; offline for selected languages after you download a pack |
| Trains | **KORAIL+** | Buy KTX tickets; bookings normally open at 07:00 two months ahead |
| Entry | **K-ETA** | The official K-ETA application, alongside k-eta.go.kr |
| Taxis | **k.ride** | Kakao Mobility's app for visitors, in English, Chinese and Japanese |
| Taxis | **Uber** | Calls an Uber Taxi with your existing account; translates messages to the driver |
| Taxis | **TABA** | Taxi app that takes Visa, Mastercard, UnionPay and JCB |
| Paying | **WOWPASS** | Prepaid card for visitors: money exchange, payment and transport |
| Safety | **Emergency Ready** | Disaster information in 22 languages, with alerts for your region |
| Safety | **Baro Emergency Reporting** | Report an emergency by text or image |

Source: each app's official listing or operator page (linked below); checked Oct 22–25, 2026.

## Getting around

### Naver Map

Made by NAVER Corp., Naver Map gives transit directions with real-time departure and arrival times, walking directions and car navigation, with maps in Korean, English, Japanese and Chinese. In our own web test on Oct 22, 2026, Google Maps showed transit routes in Seoul but no walking or driving directions for the route we checked.

Source: [Naver Map App Store listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/naver-map-navigation/id311867728); checked Oct 22, 2026. Full guide: [how to use Naver Map](/how-to-use-naver-map-korea/).

### KORAIL+

Korail sells KTX tickets on its website, in the KORAIL+ app, at ticket machines and at train stations, but not at subway stations. Tickets normally go on sale at 07:00, two months before your travel date.

Source: [Korail — ticketing guide](https://www.korail.com/global/eng/passengerGuide/ticketTypes/tickets); checked Oct 25, 2026. Full guide: [how to book the KTX](/how-to-book-ktx-korea/).

### Taxi apps: k.ride, Uber and TABA

| App | What the official pages say |
|---|---|
| **k.ride** | Kakao Mobility's version of Kakao T for visitors: English, Chinese and Japanese; sign in with Google or Apple; register an overseas credit card |
| **Uber** | Use the Uber app you already have to call an Uber Taxi; messages to the driver are translated automatically |
| **TABA** | Visa, Mastercard, UnionPay and JCB; covers Seoul and nearby areas, Incheon, Jeju, Chuncheon, Wonju, Daejeon, Gumi, Gwangju, Gimhae and Changwon |

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — Taxi](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140661) and [TABA](https://www.tabataxi.app/); checked Oct 25, 2026. Fares and tips: [taxis in Korea](/taxis-in-korea/).

> **Local tip:** If you book through TABA, the app charges your card. TABA warns that paying the driver in cash as well means you pay twice.

## Language

### Papago

Papago is NAVER Corp.'s translator. Its official listing names 14 languages, including English, Japanese, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), Spanish, French, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, Russian, German, Italian and Arabic.

| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| Image translation | Take a photo, and Papago translates the text in it (menus, signs) |
| Voice translation | Speak, and get the translation in real time |
| Conversation | A 1:1 conversation where each person speaks their own language |
| Offline | On supported devices, after you download an offline language pack while online: Korean, English, Japanese and Simplified Chinese only |

Offline text translation is available on supported devices after you download an offline language pack while online. It supports Korean, English, Japanese and Simplified Chinese; NAVER's help page lists 4 GB of RAM or more for the device. Image, conversation, website and document translation don't work offline. Papago also works in a browser at papago.naver.com.

Source: [Papago App Store listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/naver-papago-ai-translator/id1147874819) and [Papago help — offline translation](https://help.naver.com/service/16448/bookmark/10663?osType=MOBILE) (Korean); checked Oct 25, 2026.

> **Our take:** Install Papago and download the offline language pack you need while you still have internet access. Check that your language pair and device are supported before your trip. See [eSIM, SIM or pocket Wi-Fi](/esim-sim-card-pocket-wifi-korea/).

## Entry and paying

### K-ETA

If you need a K-ETA, apply only on k-eta.go.kr or the official K-ETA app; the government warns about lookalike sites that charge extra. 22 countries and regions are temporarily exempt until December 31, 2026 (Korea time).

Source: [K-ETA](https://www.k-eta.go.kr/portal/guide/viewetaapplication.do); checked Oct 23, 2026. Full guide: [K-ETA explained](/k-eta-korea/).

### WOWPASS

Its operator, Orange Square, Inc., describes WOWPASS as "an all-in-one prepaid card for foreign travelers in Korea, covering money exchange, payment, transportation, and brand rewards." Check fees and limits in the app before you load money.

Source: [WOWPASS App Store listing](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/wowpass-go-cashless-in-korea/id1626691440); checked Oct 23, 2026. More on cards and cash: [paying in Korea](/paying-in-korea-foreign-cards-cash/).

## Safety

| App | Run by | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Emergency Ready** | Ministry of the Interior and Safety | Disaster information in 22 languages, including English, Chinese and Japanese; choose your region and disaster-alert settings |
| **Baro Emergency Reporting** | Ministry of the Interior and Safety | Report an emergency by text or image; in English, Chinese, Japanese, Vietnamese, Filipino and more |

Source: [Seoul Metropolitan Government — Emergency Ready App](https://english.seoul.go.kr/service/living/disaster-evacuation-tips-citizens/emergency-ready-app/) and [Korea Tourism Organization — disaster safety services](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?menuSn=177&vcontsId=248145); checked Oct 25, 2026. Numbers to save: [emergency help in Korea](/emergency-help-korea/).

> **Local tip:** The 1330 Korea Travel Helpline isn't an app you need to install: you can call it (+82-2-1330 from overseas) or chat through 1330 Messenger, KakaoTalk, Line or WhatsApp, daily from 07:00 to midnight Korea time.

## Before you fly

1. Install Naver Map and Papago, and download Papago's offline pack if your language pair is supported.
2. Install KORAIL+ if you'll take the KTX.
3. Set up one taxi app with your card (k.ride, Uber or TABA).
4. Need a K-ETA? Use only k-eta.go.kr or the official K-ETA app.
5. Add Emergency Ready and Baro Emergency Reporting.

Source: the official listings and operator pages linked above; checked Oct 22–25, 2026.

## FAQ

### What is the best map app for Korea?

We recommend Naver Map. It gives transit, walking and driving directions with English maps. In our Oct 22, 2026 web test, Google Maps showed no walking or driving directions for the Seoul route we checked.

### Which translation app works in Korea?

Papago, by NAVER Corp. It translates text, photos and speech across 14 languages. Offline translation works for Korean, English, Japanese and Simplified Chinese on supported devices, after you download a language pack.

### Can I call a taxi in Korea with an English app?

Yes. k.ride works in English, Chinese and Japanese and takes overseas cards; TABA lets you search addresses in any language and takes Visa, Mastercard, UnionPay and JCB; and Uber calls an Uber Taxi with your existing account and translates messages to the driver.

### Is there an official K-ETA app?

Yes. The government says to apply only on k-eta.go.kr or the official K-ETA app.

# Korean Etiquette for Travelers: Restaurants, Table Manners and the Subway

URL: https://realkoreatrip.com/korean-etiquette/
Last checked: 2026-10-25

## Quick answer

- Tipping is generally not expected. The Korea Tourism Organization says tipping isn't required or expected in Korea, and asking for more water or the complimentary side dishes costs nothing extra.
- At the table, follow the oldest person. Korea.net's guide says younger people usually wait for elders to start eating, and use both hands when pouring or receiving a drink from someone older.
- On the subway, let people off first and keep your voice down. Seoul Metro also asks riders to offer seats to pregnant women, people with children and the physically disadvantaged.

**Three basics for visitors to Korea: tipping is generally not expected (the Korea Tourism Organization says it isn't required or expected), follow the oldest person's lead at the table, and on the subway let people off first and keep your voice down.** Korea.net's guide also says many households eat quite casually. If you're unsure, follow your host's lead. Below: restaurants, table manners and Seoul Metro's 10 subway rules, each from an official source.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — About Korean Food](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140727), [Korea.net — table manners](https://www.korea.net/NewsFocus/Society/view?articleId=175173) and [Seoul Metro — etiquette](http://www.seoulmetro.co.kr/en/page.do?menuIdx=645); checked Oct 25, 2026.

![Graphic: Korean etiquette at a glance — no tipping, free refills, wait for elders, both hands for drinks, let passengers off first](/img/etiquette-steps.png?v=e6537118 "Korean etiquette at a glance. Details and sources below.")

## The short version

| Where | Do | Don't |
|---|---|---|
| Restaurants | If there's a call bell, press it for service; ask for more water or complimentary side dishes (free) | Expect to tip: it isn't required or expected |
| At the table | Let older people start eating first; use both hands when pouring or receiving a drink from someone older | Stick chopsticks upright in rice; lift your rice or soup bowl; blow your nose at the table |
| Subway | Let passengers off before you board; keep to the right in stations; offer your seat to those who need it | Push on crowded trains; speak loudly |

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140727), [Korea.net](https://www.korea.net/NewsFocus/Society/view?articleId=175173) and [Seoul Metro](http://www.seoulmetro.co.kr/en/page.do?menuIdx=645); checked Oct 25, 2026.

## At a restaurant

| | What the Korea Tourism Organization says |
|---|---|
| Tipping | "Tipping is not required or expected in Korea." |
| Refills | More water or the complimentary side dishes don't cost extra; check the menu for anything ordered separately |
| Self-service | More restaurants let you serve your own water and side dishes, or order at a kiosk |
| Call bell | If provided, press the table's call button when you need a server (its guide notes it can be loud) |
| Cutlery | Its guide says tables have a small drawer with spoons, chopsticks and napkins |
| Storage chairs | Some chairs open up to store your coat and bag away from food smells |

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization — About Korean Food](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140727) (page updated Mar 24, 2023); checked Oct 25, 2026. What to order: [what to eat in Jeonju](/what-to-eat-in-jeonju/) and [Busan](/busan-travel-guide/).

## Table manners

Korea.net, the government's official English site, runs a guide to table manners for visitors. Its main points:

| Situation | The custom |
|---|---|
| Setting the table | Rice on the left and soup on the right; the spoon on the left and chopsticks on the right |
| Eating with elders | Younger people usually wait until the older people at the table pick up their spoons and start |
| Drinks with elders | Hold the cup or bottle with both hands when pouring for or receiving from someone older, and turn slightly away when you drink |
| Chopsticks | Don't stick them upright in a bowl of rice: that is done in rituals for the dead |
| Bowls | Don't lift your rice or soup bowl while eating |
| Manners | Don't pick your teeth or blow your nose during a meal |

The same guide notes that not talking during meals was the etiquette in the past, and that many households now eat quite casually.

Source: [Korea.net — While in Korea, Episode 7: Table manners](https://www.korea.net/NewsFocus/Society/view?articleId=175173) (culture series, Sep 12, 2019); checked Oct 25, 2026.

> **Our take:** If you're unsure, watch the oldest person at the table and follow their pace. Using both hands for a drink with an older person is an easy gesture to get right.

## On the subway

Seoul Metro lists 10 basic rules for riders:

1. Don't push and shove on a crowded train.
2. Let passengers get off the train before you board.
3. Offer your seat to pregnant women, people with children and the physically disadvantaged.
4. Don't walk or run on an escalator.
5. Put your phone on vibrate and keep your voice down on calls.
6. Don't buy things from peddlers on trains.
7. Don't run or speak loudly on trains.
8. Fold your newspaper for others, or take it with you when you get off.
9. Keep to the right when walking in stations.
10. Don't try to ride without paying.

> **Local tip:** Seoul Metro also asks riders not to rush for a train when its doors are about to close. Wait for the next one instead, and before you step on, check that the train is heading toward your destination.

Source: [Seoul Metro — Subway etiquette](http://www.seoulmetro.co.kr/en/page.do?menuIdx=645); checked Oct 25, 2026. Fares and transfers: [Seoul subway guide](/seoul-subway-guide/).

## Before you go

1. Tipping is generally not expected, so there's no need to budget for it.
2. At a meal with older people, let them start first, and use both hands for drinks.
3. Don't leave chopsticks standing in your rice.
4. On the subway, let people off first, keep your voice down and keep to the right in stations.
5. Need help explaining something? The 1330 Korea Travel Helpline interprets daily from 07:00 to midnight Korea time.

Source: [Korea Tourism Organization](https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140727), [Korea.net](https://www.korea.net/NewsFocus/Society/view?articleId=175173), [Seoul Metro](http://www.seoulmetro.co.kr/en/page.do?menuIdx=645) and our [emergency help guide](/emergency-help-korea/); checked Oct 25, 2026.

## FAQ

### Do you tip in Korea?

No. The Korea Tourism Organization says tipping is not required or expected, and extra water or side dishes don't cost more.

### What should I not do with chopsticks in Korea?

Don't stick them upright in a bowl of rice. Korea.net's guide explains that this is done in rituals for the dead.

### How do I drink with older people in Korea?

Hold the cup or bottle with both hands when pouring for or receiving from someone older, and turn slightly away when you drink.

### What are the rules on the Seoul subway?

Seoul Metro asks riders to let passengers off first, offer seats to pregnant women, people with children and the physically disadvantaged, keep their voice down and keep to the right in stations.

## Sources

- Korea Tourism Organization — About Korean Food (visiting a restaurant): https://english.visitkorea.or.kr/svc/contents/contentsView.do?vcontsId=140727
- Korea.net — While in Korea, Episode 7: Table manners: https://www.korea.net/NewsFocus/Society/view?articleId=175173
- Seoul Metro — Subway etiquette: http://www.seoulmetro.co.kr/en/page.do?menuIdx=645
